items.content:
Nick Haymes’s intimate portrait of his family’s life

  • Tuesday 1 September, 2026
  • Text by Miss Rosen
  • Photography by Nick Haymes
Add as a preferred source Apple News Instagram
Nick Haymes’s intimate portrait of his family’s life
Miss Rosen
Chronograph — Over 25 years, the photographer documented his son’s lives as they grew into adults. The resulting photobook is an exploration of the passage of time, as well as the optimism of youth.

Chronograph — Over 25 years, the photographer documented his son’s lives as they grew into adults. The resulting photobook is an exploration of the passage of time, as well as the optimism of youth.

Photographer Nick Haymes​’s newest book, Chronograph (SPBH Editions), opens on September 11 just moments after the North Tower was hit, the crystal blue sky slowly filling with ominous clouds of smoke. ​“That was the end of the 21st century before it even began,” he says.

Realising life is short, Haymes and his partner Lina began their life with her young son, Philipp, and soon welcomed Lawrence, a boy of their own, into the family. As a stay at home father, Haymes lived by Dad Code. ​“I never spoke to them as kids,” he says. ​“They’re always spoken to as adults, and then we figured it out. I’m not one of those parents who follow them down a slide. If they’re going to go break their nose, they can. You do it once, and then you never do it again.” 

His ​“live and let live” ethos created space for self discovery at every age, the every day moments of his children’s lives evoking the freewheeling spirit of Pee-wee’s Playhouse. ​“Everyone becomes extended family and ends up in our house at some point so there is always a crossover,” says Haymes, who has introduced his children to muses like Love Bailey and Gabe, who have inspired his previous monographs. 

  • Read next: An unconventional portrait of queer motherhood

Haymes’s love for the next generation lies at the core of his work. ​“I photograph youth culture because there’s something intrinsically fantastic about it,” he says. ​“There is an optimism that at some point you lose. It’s like, oh my God, the world is falling apart, what are we going to do? But at some point you’ll listen to a 20-year-old, and think, maybe you’re right, maybe it can change, and why not? It’s good to hear.” 

With Chronograph, Haymes devoted a quarter of a century to photographing his family, allowing the story to unfold at the natural pace of life, while his publisher Bruno Ceschel waited patiently for 15 years until the story was complete. Bookended by death – collective and personal – Haymes reimagines the domestic narrative through the lens of fatherhood, a vantage point unexplored despite the preponderance of men across all disciplines of the photo industry. 

For the better part of photography history, the domestic interior has been largely disregarded as a serious space, in no small part due to the fact it has been dominated by women artists such as Sally Mann, Tina Barney, Melonie Bennett, Judith Black, and Susan Kandel. But in more recent years, institutions have finally embraced what visionaries have always known: our first, most profound experience of photography is the family photo album. Here we discover ourselves and loved ones cast against the backdrop of ancestry and lineage cast among snapshots of moments both grand and intimate.

  • Read next: Motoyuki Daifu’s chaotic vision of the Japanese family home

“This isn’t a book on parenthood. It’s more a book about existence, understanding, and appreciating the time you have on the planet and how you spend it.” Haymes says. ​“If you’re going to have kids, you may as well be active in their lives in some form. I never wanted to censor them. Same as that, I never used a pacifier; I think that’s just wrong because for the rest of your whole life, you’re told to shut up and get in line.”

Chronograph (2026) by Nick Haymes published by SPBH Editions / MACK.

Miss Rosen is a freelance arts and photography writer, follow her on X.

items.content:
Kristina Rozhkova’s scatty, confronting portrait of captivity

  • Friday 28 August, 2026
  • Text by Isaac Muk
  • Photography by Kristina Rozhkova
Add as a preferred source Apple News Instagram
Kristina Rozhkova’s scatty, confronting portrait of captivity
Isaac Muk
Gut Feeling — The Russian artist’s arrest and subsequent detention in 2024 opened her eye towards the omnipresent dynamics of power and control. Her new photobook is a stark exploration of being trapped.

Gut Feeling — The Russian artist’s 2024 arrest and subsequent detention opened her eye towards the omnipresent dynamics of power and control. Her new photobook is a stark exploration of being trapped.

On June 19, 2024, Kristina Rozhkova was arrested in Russia alongside three others – Anna Panteleeva, Yaroslava Guminaya, and Sergey Evstyukhin. First, they were taken to a temporary detention centre (IVS), before Rozhkova was transferred to a pre-trial detention (SIZO) facility for two months. For the next year and a half, she had to attend ​“endless” court hearings.

It came after a photoshoot they had organised in a Russian Orthodox cemetery. ​“There were no victims, no damaged property and no physical evidence,” she says. ​“It featured elements of shibari [Japanese rope bondage], which was a technique I frequently incorporated into my work. We wore structured outfits, and the focus was entirely aesthetic rather than overtly political – there was nothing vulgar or inherently provocative.”

But Rozhkova claims that the group were the targets of a co-ordinated attack from a group known as Muzhskoye Gosudarstvo, which translates to ​‘Male State’, who reported them to the authorities, even though none of the final photographs had been published. It came after one of the models in the shoot had publicly called out a male artist for sexual assault prior to the shoot.

  • Read next: In a world of noise, IC3PEAK are finding radicality in the quiet

The only thing that had surfaced in public was a leaked screenshot of a behind the scenes video. ​“It was terrible. Being in SIZO at first was completely unbearable – those two months were genuinely agonizing,” she recalls. ​“My cellmates used to tell me that the first two months are always the hardest period to survive, and after that, it gradually becomes easier to manage month by month.”

House arrest was hardly easier. ​“At first, house arrest felt like absolute paradise – you sleep in a normal bed, watch movies, read and focus on hobbies,” she continues. ​“But after two months, I realised it was its own form of hell. I couldn’t go for a walk or step outside, and I had to watch my life pass me by without understanding why.”

That period, which ultimately consumed two years of her life, without considering the long-term mental effects since, inspired her to create her series and newly published photobook Gut Feeling. Its photographs – which are scatty, disquieting and occasionally even violent – explore the physical experience of being trapped with no control or way out. Photos with chains and ropes are sequenced alongside people physically holding others down – one shot sees a person squatting, with their feet obscuring a man’s face.

  • Read next: Tender, carefree portraits of young Ukrainians before the war

Animals also play a key theme in the book. There are mice in jars, a goose being restrained, and references to horses and dogs throughout. Growing up, Rozhkova was surrounded by them – her mother was a dog breeder, and she regularly attended dog shows. Her first friend was a bull terrier, and she described her childhood as Mowgli-like. Her arrest brought back many of those memories and sharpened her focus on the relationship between animals and humans.

“Being confined created a very specific physical and psychological feeling – one I later tried to recreate in my work – of being a trapped animal in a tiny cage,” Rozhkova explains. ​“Imagine putting vastly different species into one tight space. If you keep animals of the same kind together under proper conditions, they might get along, like getting a second dog so the first one isn’t lonely. But SIZO was a forced mixing of completely incompatible human lives in atrocious conditions. The environment was so wretched that everyone became overwhelmed by aggression, rage and sickness. It was utterly inhumane.”

Yet Rozhkova’s arrest didn’t come in isolation. The past decade and a half have seen the Russian authorities increasingly clamp down on dissenting voices and artists in particular – notably beginning with the arrest of punk group Pussy Riot in 2012, but intensifying in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. According to Human Rights Watch, as of July 2026, there were 1,715 political prisoners in the country, which was up by 997 from a year before.

  • Read next: Analogue Appreciation: Maria Teriaeva’s five pieces that remind her of home

“Before COVID-19, things in the country felt relatively normal – neither I nor my circle felt any heavy pressure,” she says. ​“The turning point came after the pandemic, but the real nightmare began when the full-scale war started. From then on, literally with every passing month and day, the circle was tightening faster and faster. Authorities started raiding art exhibitions, closing entire museums and controlling art fairs to remove specific works. It became glaringly obvious how impossible it was for artists to truly express themselves.”

The photographs ultimately speak to more than just her arrest, but the array of power dynamics that dominate human existence on earth. Whether it’s parents with their children, husbands and wives, rich and poor, governments with populations, people and pets, or the livestock industry at large, there are structural imbalances that govern our everyday lives.

“I see the project as universal. It can be interpreted through everyday, intimate, sexual or deeply personal lenses,” she says. ​“Totalitarian frameworks and mechanics of control exist everywhere – within medical institutions, schools and universities.”

  • Read next: In photos: Inmates of the oldest women’s prison in the USA

Like many other young, creative people of her generation, Rozhkova now lives outside of Russia. Around 1,000,000 people are believed to have emigrated since February 2022, mostly under the age of 45. Yet while she hopes the future holds an end to the war and a free Russia, her life has been changed forever.

“Before I was arrested, I could never have imagined that something like this would happen to me, or how brutal the reality of it is,” she continues. ​“Once you’ve been through it, you can no longer trust the world in the same way. It fundamentally shatters your trust in society, in authorities, and in safety itself.”

Gut Feeling by Kristina Rozhkova is published by VOID.

From BeBop to Illusion — Valiéndose del cristal como medio para iluminar las distintas capas de la ciudad, el veterano fotógrafo y cineasta publica su primera monografía a los 86 años.

From BeBop to Illusion — Valiéndose del cristal como medio para iluminar las distintas capas de la ciudad, el veterano fotógrafo y cineasta publica su primera monografía a los 86 años.

Para el fotógrafo Shawn Walker, la vida no es en blanco y negro, sino una sinfonía de texturas y tonalidades, superpuestas como los ritmos, armonías y melodías de su ciudad natal. Nacido en Harlem en 1940, Walker dio sus primeros pasos acompañando a su tío, Herbert Hoover, un fotógrafo de bares y clubes que fue de los primeros en el barrio en tener una Polaroid. A finales de los años ​50, frecuentaba míticos clubes de jazz como Minton’s Playhouse y Birdland, mientras practicaba con su propio instrumento: la cámara fotográfica. 

Al observar la próspera actividad paralela de su tío, Walker comprendió de manera intuitiva que podía hacer fotografías sin depender de ellas como medio de vida. Se unió a un grupo local de fotografía que en 1963 se fusionó con otro para dar origen a Kamoinge, hoy el colectivo fotográfico sin fines de lucro más antiguo del mundo. A Walker, el miembro fundador más joven, se sumaron figuras de la talla de Roy DeCarava, Adger Cowans, Anthony Barboza y, más adelante, Ming Smith y Frank Stewart. 

Fue allí, en los hogares de los miembros de Kamoinge durante sus apasionadas sesiones dominicales, donde Walker aprendió que la fotografía no era solo un oficio, sino un arte. No había más reglas que las que él mismo pudiera escribir, y así lo hizo, dedicando toda una vida a elevar la fotografía al rango de las bellas artes. En 2019, Walker se convirtió en el primer fotógrafo negro cuyo archivo fue adquirido por la Biblioteca del Congreso de los Estados Unidos; su colección de más de 100 000 imágenes reposa junto al legado de grandes figuras como Toni Morrison, James Baldwin y Maya Angelou, a quienes retrató a lo largo de su ilustre trayectoria de siete décadas.

En imágenes: La resistencia perdurable del Carnaval de Notting Hill
Isaac Muk
Carnival of Resistance — Un nuevo fotolibro de Wayne Campbell y Wayne Crichlow reflexiona sobre los orígenes contestatarios del mayor festival callejero de Europa, junto con las tradiciones que mantienen vivo hoy su espíritu original.

Carnival of Resistance — Un nuevo fotolibro de Wayne Campbell y Wayne Crichlow reflexiona sobre los orígenes contestatarios del mayor festival callejero de Europa, junto con las tradiciones que mantienen vivo hoy su espíritu original.

El Carnaval de Notting Hill siempre despierta imágenes nítidas en el imaginario colectivo. Carrozas de una elaboración minuciosa. Los atuendos multicolores y emplumados de las comparsas. El estruendo ensordecedor de reggae, dub, jungle y UK garage de los soundsystems. Pollo jerk, curry de cabra y arroz con guisantes. Multitudes inmensas y palpitantes que desfilan por las calles del barrio. O bien, para sus detractores, encarna el desorden, el ruido y un caos incontrolable para la policía.

Sin embargo, con menor frecuencia se recuerda su dimensión como acto de protesta. En 1958, estallaron graves y violentos disturbios raciales en este barrio del oeste de Londres, cuando turbas de pandillas blancas armadas con palos, botellas, ladrillos y cuchillos atacaron los hogares y comercios de la comunidad negra. Como respuesta, un año después, en 1959, la periodista y activista Claudia Jones —nacida en Trinidad y Tobago y radicada en el Reino Unido tras haber sido encarcelada en los Estados Unidos durante la ​«Caza de brujas» anticomunista— organizó una fiesta en el ayuntamiento de St Pancras.

Hubo bandas de steelpans, cantantes y bailarines: una celebración cultural que respondió a la violencia y al racismo a través de la música y la danza. Aquel acontecimiento sentó las bases de la resistencia a través del júbilo y la exaltación de la cultura, lo que finalmente inspiró el primer Carnaval oficial de Notting Hill en 1966. ​«El asesinato de Kelso Cochrane [migrante de Antigua] estaba fracturando a las comunidades», explica el fotógrafo Wayne Campbell, coautor del nuevo fotolibro Carnival of Resistance, publicado coincidiendo con la conmemoración de los 60 años de historia del festival.

Manami Okazaki
Noches de Asakusa — A pesar de los incontables incendios y el endurecimiento de las leyes sobre el trabajo sexual, esta zona con siglos de historia sigue en pie en el este de Tokio. Manami Okazaki recorre su historia y se adentra en las vidas de quienes moldean su presente.

Los soaplands de Asakusa — A pesar de los numerosos incendios y el endurecimiento de las leyes sobre el trabajo sexual, esta zona con siglos de historia continúa resistiendo en el este de Tokio. Manami Okazaki recorre su historia y se adentra en las vidas de quienes moldean su presente.

Cae la tarde en Yoshiwara, una notable cuadrícula urbana al norte de Asakusa, en el este de Tokio, a un tiro de piedra del templo Senso-ji, una de las atracciones turísticas más frecuentadas de Japón. Las calles rezuman una relativa quietud, pero ante la mayoría de los edificios aguardan furgonetas negras de lunas tintadas y proliferan los aparcamientos. Los burdeles se suceden pared con pared —alrededor de 140—, iluminados por rótulos de estética ochentera con neones palpitantes donde se leen nombres como ​«Moulin Rouge», ​«Etoile» y ​«Good Wife». Porteros trajeados custodian las entradas, mientras mujeres, en su mayoría veinteañeras, cruzan los umbrales. 

A pesar de que Yoshiwara está considerado el principal barrio rojo de Japón —donde la mayoría de los locales de lujo cobran entre 80 000 ¥ (370 £) y 100 000 ¥ (460 £) por 120 minutos—, el lugar parece un enclave detenido en el tiempo. Sus inmuebles se yerguen como reliquias de la era de la burbuja financiera, impregnados de un halo retro y kitsch; la atmósfera entera del distrito evoca el fotograma de una película ambientada en una década perdida, justo antes del descalabro económico. 

El propio Yoshiwara atesora una historia legendaria que se remonta al periodo Edo (1600-1868), cuando fue concebido por el sogunato para confinar el floreciente comercio carnal dentro de un perímetro delimitado. Fundado originariamente en Ningyocho, fue trasladado a su emplazamiento actual en Senzoku después de que un pavoroso incendio lo redujera a cenizas. El fuego ha arrasado Yoshiwara en incontables ocasiones, pero el barrio siempre ha vuelto a levantarse, sobreviviendo incluso a la ilegalización de la prostitución en 1958. 

A causa de las normativas vigentes sobre negocios de entretenimiento para adultos, abrir nuevos prostíbulos en la zona es prácticamente inviable, por lo que muchos de los edificios se restauran en lugar de demolerse y sustituirse. A ello se suman unas rigurosas leyes de zonificación que hacen casi imposible iniciar un nuevo negocio. Y aunque persiste una evidente tolerancia social hacia la industria del sexo comercial, este escenario podría tener los días contados: resulta incierto si Yoshiwara logrará sobrevivir a semejantes restricciones legales en las próximas décadas. 

  • Lectura recomendada: El intrincado y clandestino arte del tatuaje tradicional japonés

Crash Bang: el nuevo fotolibro de DB Burkeman saca a la luz fotografías de sus años de juventud como aspirante a fotógrafo musical, las cuales permanecieron sin revelar en la casa familiar durante décadas.

Crash Bang: el nuevo fotolibro de DB Burkeman saca a la luz fotografías de sus años de juventud como aspirante a fotógrafo musical, las cuales permanecieron sin revelar en la casa familiar durante décadas.

Tras la muerte de su madre, DB Burkeman regresó a la casa familiar en Londres para vaciar su habitación de la infancia. Allí descubrió una bolsa de plástico transparente con unos 30 carretes de película en blanco y negro sin revelar: vestigios de su breve pero fascinante etapa como fotógrafo de rock & roll a caballo entre los años setenta y los ochenta. ​«Los había tirado en este cajón pensando que ya me ocuparía de ellos más tarde, pero en aquella época yo era un desastre», comenta Burkeman. ​«Mi prioridad nunca fue ser fotógrafo profesional. Le decía a la gente que a eso me dedicaba, pero la realidad era [otra muy distinta]».

Criado en Londres durante los años ​70, Burkeman recuerda lo estancada que se había vuelto la cultura juvenil al ver cómo el rock de estadios producía en serie una generación de clones. ​«Antes del ​76, todo el mundo vestía igual. Era un mar de tela vaquera, ¿sabes? Pantalones de campana, chaquetas vaqueras y melenas largas», afirma. ​«De pronto se produjo un cambio sísmico: los Pistols abrieron una brecha y transformaron por completo la percepción de lo que podía ser una banda de rock. Había 100 grupos tocando cada noche en Londres y solo tenías que pagar tres libras, en lugar de 30, para ver a Eddie and the Hot Rods o a The Damned. Todo el mundo se cortó el pelo y se deshizo de los pantalones acampanados. Todo cambió de golpe».

Inspirado por esa energía, Burkeman dejó los estudios a los 16 años. Aunque más adelante se convertiría en DJ y llevaría el jungle a Nueva York en los años ​90, su talento musical permaneció latente durante su juventud. Pero no todo estaba perdido. Según explica: ​«Me fascinaba la imagen del fotógrafo; era casi como ser una estrella de rock. Eras importante, pero a la vez te resguardabas detrás de una cámara, en lugar de una guitarra o una batería».

  • Lectura recomendada: El regreso del riot grrrl: ¿es más necesario que nunca?

Encuentro celestial: Ella Glossop fotografía un acontecimiento irrepetible y el espíritu comunitario que se congregó en el norte de Londres para presenciar un momento único en décadas.

Encuentro celestial — Ella Glossop fotografía este acontecimiento único en décadas desde uno de los miradores más concurridos de la ciudad, retratando el espíritu comunitario que definió el momento.

Londres no presenciaba un eclipse solar de tal magnitud desde 1999.

Ahora, en este gran año de 2026, mientras miles de personas acuden a la cima de Primrose Hill ante el espectáculo, el ambiente aún conserva cierta esencia noventera. Quizá sea el carácter artesanal de toda la tecnología: las gafas de Meta no sirven de mucho aquí, así que reinan las lentes de plástico holográfico sujetas con cartón. Las cámaras de los móviles apenas logran retratar el sol, por lo que la gente ha traído todo tipo de equipos fotográficos, coladores y proyectores hechos con cajas de cereales. Quizá sea el hecho de que —en pleno día de verano— no estemos a 35 grados. O tal vez, a medida que el sol se oculta tras la luna y la luz se aplana, sea esa extraña sensación de que todo podría salir bien.

Un fenómeno de dos horas de duración: el eclipse alcanzó su punto culminante a las 7:13 p. m., con más del 90% del sol cubierto. No volveremos a ver una cobertura tan completa hasta 2081. El clímax desató una gran ovación entre la multitud, apiñada hombro con hombro sobre mantas de picnic, mientras se descorchaban botellas de espumoso y los radiocasetes hacían sonar música. Luego, cuando el sol volvió a asomar tras la luna y regresó la luz habitual del día, quedó una atmósfera neblinosa, similar a la de las 5 de la mañana.

  • Sigue leyendo: Danny León ejecuta un descomunal aéreo alineado con el eclipse solar

El mundo moderno es abrumador, las grandes tecnológicas son gigantescas, internet es ensordecedor... y, una vez cada varias décadas, recibimos una dosis de perspectiva avalada por el cosmos.

Ella Glossop, de Huck, estuvo allí para capturar la escena. Descubre sus fotografías a continuación.

items.content:
Surveying community and resistance in LGBTQ+ nightlife

  • Tuesday 11 August, 2026
  • Text by Miss Rosen
  • Photography by Various. See Captions.
Add as a preferred source Apple News Instagram
Linda Simpson, Linda Simpson, Gillian, Honey Dijon, and Candis Cayne at Wigstock at the Palladium, 1995. © Linda Simpson. From Sex, Clubs, Dissent: Visualising Queer Nightlife by Amelia Abraham (MACK, 2026). Courtesy of the artist and MACK.
Surveying community and resistance in LGBTQ+ nightlife
Miss Rosen
Sex, Clubs Dissent — A new book collates queer nightlife photography over the past 50 years, and the people who found refuge and safe spaces after dark.

Sex, Clubs Dissent — A new book collates queer nightlife photography over the past 50 years, and the people who found refuge and safe spaces after dark.

For over a century, queer nightlife thrived in the margins of society, driven underground by the criminalisation of sexuality and genders beyond the binary. Here in bars, clubs, ballrooms, warehouses, bathhouses, dungeons, cruising grounds, and strolls where sex is sold, generations have come together as an act of love and resistance against a world that shunned them. In those clandestine spaces, queer culture took root, becoming the lingua franca of music, style, beauty, glamour, and attitude – to say nothing of political activism and mutual aid that has saved lives and changed laws. 

Progress, however, can be a double-edged sword with the price of conditional freedom being cultural appropriation by a mainstream all too willing to erase the source. Ballroom colloquialisms like ​‘the tea’, ​‘kiki’, ​‘shade’, ​‘slay’, ​‘reading’, ​‘gagging’, and ​‘giving’ are often mislabelled as ​‘gen Z slang’ while contemporary and historic Black, brown and LGBTQ+ creators are paid dust. 

“There’s an acceleration of ubiquitous hyper capitalism and absorption of queer culture,” says author Amelia Abraham, on the phone from the streets of London. She’s just had a pop into The Photographers’ Gallery Bookshop, where her latest book, Sex, Clubs, Dissent: Visualising Queer Nightlife (MACK), is set among the new arrivals. The book’s red cover beckons with a keyhole glimpse of unbridled amour, revealed to be Meryl Meisler​’s photograph of two women on the floor of Les Mouches, a members-only queer nightclub on Manhattan’s west side in the late 1970s. It’s a delectable promise of things to come. 

  • Read next: Inside Parkuir: the art project queering sport, space and our bodies

In Sex, Clubs, Dissent, Abraham explores the intersections of community, creativity, desire, and liberation, spotlighting the originators and innovators who blazed their own paths over half a century. Bringing together the work of artists including David Wojnarowicz, Sunil Gupta, Mariette Pathy Allen, Bruce LaBruce, Reynaldo Rivera, Linda Simpson, Lyle Ashton Harris, Clifford Prince King, and Chloe Sherman, the book is a panoramic landscape of the power and pride that’s only found when the night comes alive. 

Although Abraham started clubbing as a teen, it wasn’t until she discovered The Joiners Arms at the age of 21 that she finally had a place to call her own. ​“It was really chaotic. The floor was sticky with beer, the toilets were flooded, and it felt lawless and exciting to me,” she remembers fondly of the fabled Shoreditch dive bar. ​“It was loads of people from different subcultures coming together, a real melting pot, like the 60-year-old trans matriarch Stephanie, who always sat at the bar. It was one of the first places where I really fell in love with queer nightlife.” 

Drawn to the intergenerational aspect of Joiners, Abraham struck up a friendship with photographer Jeffrey Hinton, whose portrait of dancer Michael Clark, appears in the book. ​“Jeff is in his 60s and I’ve had the pleasure of hearing his stories about the nightlife that came before,” she says. ​“He has the same kind of attitude that Joiners had, which is quite DIY, egalitarian, and messy. That’s what we’re talking about with the word ​‘dissent’ – a kind of disorderliness. Fuck it! Just do it – and do it for the love of it!” 

  • Read next: An intimate window into New York’s ​’70s lesbian scene

It is this ethos that Abraham brings to the book, crafting a tour de force that is as much a photographic history as it is a family album, particularly in light of the criminalisation of queer sexuality around the globe. ​“The Gay Rights Movement started with visibility. Before that, the camera was dangerous,” she says. ​“Photographers from that time talk about how they couldn’t show their photos because someone might lose their job or their family. And that’s true for now for certain people.”

Sex, Clubs, Dissent: Visualising Queer Nightlife (2026) by Amelia Abraham published by MACK. It will have its US launch on September 8, 2026, at the Leslie-Lohman Museum of Art in New York.

items.content:
In photos: Electric nights in ’70s Japan

  • Monday 10 August, 2026
  • Text by Miss Rosen
  • Photography by Keizō Kitajima
Add as a preferred source Apple News Instagram
In photos: Electric nights in ’70s Japan
Miss Rosen
Tokyo–Koza — Keizō Kitajima’s new photobook explores the explosion of party culture of Tokyo and Okinawa during an era of rapid change in the country, as well as its stranger turns.

Tokyo–Koza — Keizō Kitajima’s new photobook explores the explosion of party culture of Tokyo and Okinawa during an era of rapid change in the country, as well as its stranger turns.

Photography emerged at the vanguard in Japan as the 1968 – 69 university protests signified the rise of the New Left amid a global revolution against Western imperialism. Liberated from the myth of ​“objectivity” and false hierarchies of form, a small group of Japanese artists and critics including Daidō Moriyama and Nakahira Takuma came together to create Provoke, a photography magazine that embraced the raw, radical, and expressionistic possibilities of the medium. 

Although Provoke only ran three issues, its legacy would inspire generations of photographers from around the globe, beginning with native son, Keizō Kitajima. ​“I began photography in the mid-1970s, around the time when the political fervour symbolised by the May 1968 Paris Uprising was beginning to subside,” he says. ​“At that time, photography was considered one of the most cutting-edge and powerful means of expression in Japan, and I was deeply impressed by it.” 

Born in 1954 in Suzaka, Nagano Prefecture, Kitajima first discovered the work of Nobuyoshi Araki and Daidō Moriyama as a teen, going on to study with the latter in 1975 at WORK SHOP Photography School, founded by members of Provoke after the magazine folded. The two established a lifelong collaboration that took root the following year with the creation of CAMP, an artist-run gallery, darkroom, and meeting space in the Shinjuku district of Tokyo. 

With Moriyama’s support, Kitajima began exploring Koza, the historical name for Okinawa City and second largest city on the island following Tokyo. ​“Okinawa has numerous US military bases, and Koza is a nightlife district catering to American soldiers,” Kitajima says. ​“When I frequented Koza, it was shortly after the Vietnam War, and the town was bustling with many returning soldiers. People from all over Southeast Asia gathered in Koza to do business with the American soldiers. Many of them, including the soldiers, carried painful experiences in their hearts. I heard a thousand sad stories and a hundred happy stories from them.” 

With the recent publication of Keizo Kitajima: Tokyo – Koza (Little Big Man Books), the artist returns to the start of his career, retracing a fascinating chapter of Japanese photography and history. The lush, oversize paperback brings together Kitajima’s early works, Photographs of Okinawa (1975 – 1979) and Tokyo 1979, to create an electric portrait of Japanese nightlife during the second half of the decade. 

In 1979, Kitajima mounted a monthly series of exhibitions at CAMP showcasing black and white photographs made around the gallery in Shinjuku Ni-chome, a former red light district, accompanied by booklets titled Photo Express: Tokyo. ​“Japan was undergoing rapid urbanisation, and I was fascinated by the image and energy of the city,” he says. ​“The city seemed like a chaotic entity where light and darkness coexisted. Wandering through the labyrinthine alleys of Tokyo, I sought an encounter with a truth that transcended good and evil.” 

Kitajima remembers the experience as a whirlwind, excitedly photographing people who frequented the area, delighting when they would come to exhibition openings when their images were hung. ​“I attempted to compress the act of shooting, production, and exhibition into a single act, presenting it with maximum volume,” he says. Kitajima transformed CAMP into a darkroom by covering the walls with rolls of photographic paper, projecting the negatives onto them, developing them with a sponge, rinsing them in a bucket of water, and opening the show the very next day in that state. 

It is only now, half a century after these two series were made, that they can be seen together as Kitajima always dreamed. ​“For me, there are no past photographs. All the photographs I take, including street photography, are in the present tense and reflect my current position,” he says. ​“I believe it’s important to repeatedly revisit the same photographs, and I continue to re-examine the photographs I’ve taken, reinterpreting them in new contexts. My photographs are always beyond me.”

Keizo Kitajima: Tokyo – Koza is published by Little Big Man Books.

items.content:
Defiance and pride in Chicano Camera Culture

  • Wednesday 5 August, 2026
  • Text by Miss Rosen
  • Photography by Various. See Captions.
Add as a preferred source Apple News Instagram
© Robert C. Buitron
Defiance and pride in Chicano Camera Culture
Miss Rosen
A Photographic History — A new major exhibition surveys Mexican American photography over six decades, platforming Chicano artists at a Chicano museum for the first time.

A Photographic History — A new major exhibition surveys Mexican American photography over six decades, platforming Chicano artists at a Chicano museum for the first time.

Skyrocketing to fame in the late 1970s, comedian Cheech Marin parlayed his position as one half of beloved stoner duo Cheech & Chong to become one of the world’s leading proponents of Chicano (Mexican American) art. In 2022, the Cheech Marin Center for Chicano Art & Culture, aka The Cheech, opened its doors, making history as the first museum devoted exclusively to ​“all things Chicano art”.

Hailing from Los Angeles, curator Elizabeth Ferrer remembers the museum’s opening as an important event, both for the community and for herself. Recognising she was among like minds, she set forth to create Chicano Camera Culture: A Photographic History, 1966 – 2026, an epic celebration of Chicano life as seen through 150 works across multiple generations now on view at the Cheech.

Featuring nearly 50 photographers including trailblazers Louis Carlos Bernal, George Rodriguez, and María Varela; innovators Reynaldo Rivera, Kathy Vargas, and Ken Gonzales-Day; and contemporary artists Guadalupe Rosales, Star Montana, and Thalía Gochez, Chicano Camera Culture forms a map of photographic history that has been largely disregarded by industry and institutions alike. 

  • Read next: Down and out in east LA: vintage shots of Chicano life

“The photographic record, whether from the viewpoint of photojournalists, documentarians, hobbyists, or artists, was created by the white gaze, and for a long time that fact was by and large taken for granted,” Ferrer says. ​“With the rise of the Civil Rights movement, the Chicano gaze comes into play. This means that for the first time, Chicanos are representing other Chicanos, typically, people who would otherwise be anonymous or unrecognised.” 

Like Ferrer’s 2021 book, Latinx Photography in the United States: A Visual History, Chicano Camera Culture is a landmark work, exploring Chicano photography as a cultural ethos born from knowledge of self. Rather than ascribe descriptors to identity, Ferrer maps its expression across generations, exploring the age-old questions of the human condition with a tender heart and a knowing eye. 

“All of the work in the show illuminates in one way or another, what it means to be Chicano,” she says. ​“Many of the themes addressed by the photographers – pride in identity, our struggle for agency and autonomy, the values we place in family and home, and the ways we create and claim space – are unsurprising. But what is impressive is the innovative ways in which they have been elaborated.” 

  • Read next: Vibrant photos of L.A.’s contemporary lowrider culture

Organised around themes of self/​portraiture, domestic life, protests, border stories, and alternate realities, Chicano Camera Culture is a magnificent archive of collective resistance against an occupying force that has vilified and criminalised indigenous and mestizo communities, while telling the stories of the people and their cultures.

“From the beginning, the Chicano gaze has been about expressing pride in Chicano identity, preserving our history, uplifting cultural and spiritual values, validating persons out of the mainstream, and giving visibility to members of our own community,” Ferrer says. ​“As for what it means to tell Chicano stories by Chicano artists in a Chicano museum in the United States in 2026, I’d say it’s high time!” 

Chicano Camera Culture: A Photographic History, 1966 – 2026 is on view through September 6, 2026, at the Cheech Marin Art Center in Riverside, California. The catalogue is distributed by the Washington University Press for the Riverside Art Museum.
